Good news: the partners liked the idea of one evening at the gallery. Before we sign, though, there are a few rules we have to follow.
Of course. I read the policy last night. The sponsorship must be approved by the board, because it is above five thousand dollars.
Exactly. And there is something I am required to tell you. The caterer for the evening is owned by my brother-in-law.
Thank you for telling me. That is a conflict of interest, so the disclosure must be made before the vote, not after.
I agree. I will put it in writing today. Do I have to leave the meeting when the board votes?
You do not have to leave the room, but you must not vote on the caterer. Somebody else should choose it.
Fair enough. And the gallery? Our auditors will ask about them.
We did our due diligence last month. I can send you the report, so the audit committee has everything it needs.
You do not have to attend, but you must read the minutes.
If you are not sure, you must ask before you act.

When I tell people I work in compliance, they usually think of a long list of things they are not allowed to do. I understand why. But that is not what the rules are for. The rules protect the honest people in the company. If there is a clear policy on gifts, an honest manager does not have to decide alone, at a dinner, whether a present is too expensive. The policy has already decided for him. So I ask every new manager to remember only one rule, even if they forget everything else. If you are not sure, you must ask before you act, not after. Asking before costs five minutes. Explaining after can cost a career.

A few years ago a supplier sent me an expensive watch, the week after we signed a contract with them. My first thought was that it was not a problem. The contract was already signed, so the gift could not change my decision. That was wrong. Our policy said that managers must not accept gifts above one hundred dollars, at any time. There was no exception for after the signature. A colleague saw the box on my desk and asked me about it. In the end I had to return the watch, and I was required to disclose it to the audit committee. Nobody punished me. But I learned that a rule does not ask what you were thinking. It asks what you did.

First, you check the policy to see if the sponsorship needs an approval. Then, you do your due diligence on the partner before you sign anything. After that, every manager discloses any conflict of interest before the vote. Next, the board votes, and nobody with a conflict votes on that point. Finally, you keep a written record, so that the audit committee has oversight of the payment.
